{{smaller block|<poem>Therfore take hede bothe nyȝt & day
How fast ȝoure ''ȝouthe'' dooth asswage.</poem>
{{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 79.}}}}
'''3.''' A young person; especially, a young man. In this sense it has a plural.
{{smaller block|<poem>I gave it to a ''youth'',
A kind of boy.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., v. 1. 161.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Seven ''youths'' from Athens yearly sent.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, vi. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>For what in nature’s dawn the child admired,
The ''youth'' endeavoured, and the man acquired.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', To Sir Godfrey Kneller, l. 144.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Just at the age ’twixt boy and ''youth'',
When thought is speech, and speech is truth.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, ii., Int.}}}}
{{smaller block|I had hardly ever seen a handsome ''youth;'' never in my life spoken to one. {{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xii.}}}}
'''4.''' Young persons collectively.
{{smaller block|<poem>Forget the present Flame, indulge a new,
Single the loveliest of the am’rous ''Youth''.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', Henry and Emma.}}}}
{{smaller block|Even when our ''youth'', leaving schools and universities, enter that most important period of life.
{{right|''Burke'', Rev. in France.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>O ye! who teach the ingenuous ''youth'' of nations, . . .
I pray ye flog them upon all occasions.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Don Juan, ii. 1.}}}}
'''5†.''' Recentness; freshness; brief date. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Welcome hither;</poem>}}
<poem>If that the ''youth'' of my new interest here
Have power to bid you welcome.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iii. 2. 224.}}}}

'''youthede†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''youthhead.''

'''youthful''' (yöth′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ''youth'' + ''-ful.'']   '''1.''' Possessing or characterized by youth; not yet aged; not yet arrived at mature years; being in the early stage of life; young; juvenile.
{{smaller block|<poem>It was a ''youthful'' knight
Lov’d a gallant lady.</poem>
{{right|''Constance of Cleveland'' (Child’s Ballads, IV. 226).}}}}
{{smaller block|As Clifford’s young manhood had been lost, he was fond of feeling himself comparatively ''youthful'', now, in apposition with the patriarchal age of Uncle Venner.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, x.}}}}
'''2.''' Pertaining or belonging or suitable to the early part of life: as, ''youthful'' days; ''youthful'' age.
{{smaller block|<poem>His ''youthful'' hose, well saved, a world too wide
For his shrunk shank.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 7. 160.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Now no more shall these smooth brows be begirt
With ''youthful'' coronals, and lead the dance.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The discrepancy . . . between her age, which was about seventy, and her dress, which would have been ''youthful'' for twenty-seven. {{right|''Dickens'', Dombey and Son, xxi.}}}}
{{smaller block|Sometimes . . . the ''youthful'' spirit has come over me in such a rush of young blood that it has surprised me as much as the slaughtered Duncan’s manifestation surprised Lady Macbeth.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Over the Teacups, xii.}}}}

'''3.''' Fresh and vigorous, as in youth.
{{smaller block|Perfect felicity, such as after millions of millions of ages is still ''youthful'' and flourishing.
{{right|''Bentley.''}}}}

'''4.''' Early in time.
{{smaller block|<poem>Here, as I point my sword, the sun arises,
Which is a great way growing on the south,
Weighing the ''youthful'' season of the year.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., ii. 1. 108.}}}}
{{smaller block|Nor of the larger stature & cubites of men in those ''youthfull'' times and age of the world.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 39.}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn. 1-3.''' ''Youthful, Juvenile, Boyish, Puerile. Youthful'' is generally used in a good sense: as, ''youthful'' looks or sports; ''juvenile'' indifferently, but if in a bad sense not strongly so: as, the poem was a rather ''juvenile'' performance; ''boyish'' rather more often, but not necessarily, in some contempt: as, a ''boyish'' manner; ''boyish'' enthusiasm; ''puerile'' always in marked contempt, as a synonym for ''silly''.}}

'''youthfullity''' (yöth′fu̇l-i̤-ti), ''n.''   [< ''youthful'' + ''-ity''.]   Youthfulness. [Nonce-word.]
{{smaller block|You see my impetuosity does not abate much; no, nor my ''youthfullity. Walpole'', Letters (1763), II. 461. (''Davies.'')}}

'''youthfulness''' (yöth′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being youthful.

Delite so doth his bridil leede.</poem>

{{right|''Ramsay'', Vertue and Vyce, st. 37.}}}}

Some 14 genera have been placed in this family by Standinger, but the important genus ''Argyresthia'' and its allies are removed to a distinct family, ''Argyresthiidæ'', by Heinemann and others. Also ''Hyponomeutidæ''.}}

'''Y-track''' (wī′trak), ''n.'' A short track laid at right angles (or approximately so) to a line of railway, with which it is connected by two switches—the whole resembling the letter Y. {{smaller|It is used instead of a turn-table for reversing engines or cars. In}} operating it, an engine or car advancing toward ''A'' (heading as shown by the arrow) is switched at ''A'' to the track ''B'', and then backed up over the switch ''C'' to the main track again, heading now in the reverse direction.
